title: ServiceNow makes it easier to build AI agents, gives them verifiable identities
summary: ServiceNow is giving its AI Control Tower new features to make AI agents more governable — and a new name, Super Intelligence Control Tower (SICT), to please the US President. It is also updating EmployeeWorks to make building AI agents easier. AI Passport, a new component of SICT, gives every agent, whether from ServiceNow or a third party, a verifiable identity, and provides runtime control over its activities. As enterprises scale autonomous agents from pilots to production, they are facing new challenges, said Nenshad Bardoliwalla , SVP of AI product management at ServiceNow: “If companies can’t identify which agents are running, what they are doing, and what systems they can access, then scaling quickly becomes a risk.” An AI Passport is a cryptographically signed credential for AI agents that is checked at runtime to verify the scope authorized by the enterprise. When an AI agent stays within its passport scope, it can operate freely, but if it tries to deviate, defined actions are enforced. These can include redirecting, restricting, or reconnecting the agent with proper context, or even triggering a kill switch. All actions are audited so agent activity can be tracked. It is built on open specifications, so any governance product, identity provider, or enforcement point can issue and verify credentials for their own and third-party AI agents, and those credentials are verifiable at every step in multi-agent workflows. A bouncer at every door This is a real step forward, said Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research. “Most agent governance today is a security camera. It records what happened so someone can review the tape later. AI Passport is a bouncer at every door.” The controls extend beyond ServiceNow’s own agents, he said: “For third-party agents, the passport replaces the agent’s own ‘claims’ about its permissions,” he said. “Taking an agent’s word for what it is allowed to do is an Achilles’ heel of agentic AI.” And, he said, “A passport

title: Apple’s ‘Minions’ tech turns idle Macs into an AI data center
summary: If your business has lots of Macs, what do you do with them at night? And how much money do you spend on AI inferencing? What if the computational power of those Macs could be used to handle some inferencing tasks ? A new white paper from Apple’s machine learning team tells us it’s possible. Apple’s teams have developed an internal technology for distributed processing they call “Minions,” which effectively creates a virtual GPU cloud from connected Macs. While it’s not available outside Apple at this time, it seems a pretty good candidate to turn Macs into a distributed AI data center, cutting the cost of AI inferencing and making it easier for enterprises to safely analyze company data by ensuring the information stays in the company . Meet Apple’s Minions This exciting approach is described in a newly published white paper , ‘Minions: A Dynamic and Distributed Virtual GPU Cloud Built on Idle Apple Silicon Devices.” In it, the researchers explain how constrained GPU resources delay access to inference tasks and increase costs — even while powerful Macs running Apple silicon chips may sit idle. They’ve developed an approach to use that power. It’s based on three components: a Minion Server, an Executor, and a Watchdog. The server splits tasks up and puts them into a queue; the executor then acts as kind of a nightclub concierge, directing tasks across all the available Macs. The watchdog monitors active tasks and checks for failures — a Mac may be shut down or go to sleep during a task, for example. If a node goes offline, the watchdog returns that sub-task to the queue, making sure the work gets done. Minions currently supports two kinds of GPU inference on Macs, embedding generation and LLM completions using open-source transformer models from Hugging Face and Ollama, respectively. title: Arm-Qualcomm legal fight ends in limited verdict, larger stakes remain
summary: A Delaware jury found that Arm breached its licensing agreement with Qualcomm but awarded the chipmaker just $2 in damages, leaving a potentially multibillion-dollar dispute over royalty payments unresolved. The jury ruled on October 13 that Arm had failed to provide software patches and development tools required under its agreement with Qualcomm. It also found that Arm had interfered with Qualcomm’s business relationship with Meta Platforms, while rejecting several other allegations against Arm. Qualcomm is seeking to invoke a contractual provision that would allow it to stop paying royalties to Arm for five years. Arm has argued that the provision is unenforceable, leaving US District Judge Maryellen Noreika to decide whether Qualcomm is entitled to the remedy, Reuters reported. Qualcomm welcomed the finding that Arm breached its licensing obligations, while Arm emphasized that it prevailed on several other claims and was ordered to pay only nominal damages. The verdict follows an earlier dispute over Qualcomm’s 2021 acquisition of chip designer Nuvia. Arm argued that Qualcomm needed its consent to use technology developed under Nuvia’s license. A jury sided with Qualcomm on key issues in December 2024, and a judge ruled in its favor on the remaining claim in September 2025. Arm has appealed that judgment. The dispute comes as Arm expands beyond its traditional business of licensing processor technology. In March 2026, the company unveiled its first data center CPU, developed with Meta Platforms. Qualcomm, meanwhile, has been expanding beyond smartphones with its Snapdragon processors for Windows computers. PC market challenges unresolved The Arm–Qualcomm dispute is unlikely to significantly impact enterprise adoption of Snapdragon-powered Windows laptops, said Pareekh Jain , CEO of Pareekh Consulting. title: Copilot pricing gets complicated
summary: As Microsoft adds more advanced agentic capabilities to Copilot, such as Cowork and Autopilot, usage-based pricing is becoming an increasingly important part of its business model. But for customers used to predictable, fixed pricing, the addition of pay-as-you-go billing can be a significant change, creating new challenges around managing and predicting costs. Questions about the consumption pricing model are now among the most common that Gartner receives from clients around Copilot, said Max Goss, research director at Gartner. There’s “some doubt about whether a full move to consumption-based pricing for everyday knowledge work is sustainable for organizations in the long run,” he said. When Microsoft introduced Copilot three years ago, it charged businesses a flat monthly fee of $30 per user, with a $21 per user subscription later introduced for small and midsize businesses. Initial capabilities focused on helping employees find information, summarize meetings and documents, and draft content. Microsoft has since expanded Copilot with AI agents that can perform more complex tasks. Some, such as Researcher and Analyst , are included in the existing subscription, while others, including certain agents built with Copilot Studio or accessed via Copilot Chat , required usage-based charges through Copilot Credits, priced at $0.01 per credit. Now Microsoft is bringing consumption-based agents more directly into the core Copilot experience. At a recent event , it unveiled a new Home interface that places Cowork alongside the standard Chat option in the prompt box. Unlike Chat, Cowork incurs usage-based charges, with credit consumption varying depending on factors such as the model used and the complexity of the task, according to Microsoft’s pricing documentation . title: As phishing-as-a-service goes industrial, Microsoft takes down a marketplace behind 1 billion messages
summary: Microsoft says it has dismantled a criminal marketplace responsible for 1 billion malicious messages. Working with international authorities and several tech and cybersecurity companies in a nearly year-long investigation, Redmond identified and took down Yam Store, a coordinated underground network dealing in commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS). The network allowed cybercriminals to readily purchase, and very quickly deploy, pre-made kits they could use in phishing attacks to steal data and credentials. Microsoft said the takedown began as a simple investigation based on a tip from Japanese authorities. “Working together, and with the assistance of AI tools, we connected accounts, websites, and infrastructure that initially appeared unrelated, helping expose the broader criminal marketplace behind them,” Steven Masada , associate general counsel and GM for Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit, wrote in a blog post . “What appears to be a simple scam message is often the visible end of a much larger transnational cybercriminal operation.” The evolving PhaaS marketplace Collectively, YAM Store and the kits and tools sold within it enabled the sending of more than 1 billion messages to 75,000-plus organizations worldwide. More than 750 million of those were sent to Microsoft customers alone, and ultimately generated “tens of millions of dollars” for criminal operators. Investigation into the marketplace began in late 2025 after Japan’s National Police Agency (NPA) notified Microsoft of “a wave of fraud and scam activity” targeting people and businesses in Japan. Researchers expected to find multiple individual campaigns; instead, they discovered a “sprawling Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace.” The probe expanded globally and involved the efforts of several other law enforcement agencies, as well as companies like Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint, and TRM Labs. title: ServiceNow makes it easier to build AI agents, gives them verifiable identities
summary: ServiceNow is giving its AI Control Tower new features to make AI agents more governable — and a new name, Super Intelligence Control Tower (SICT), to please the US President. It is also updating EmployeeWorks to make building AI agents easier. AI Passport, a new component of SICT, gives every agent, whether from ServiceNow or a third party, a verifiable identity, and provides runtime control over its activities. As enterprises scale autonomous agents from pilots to production, they are facing new challenges, said Nenshad Bardoliwalla , SVP of AI product management at ServiceNow: “If companies can’t identify which agents are running, what they are doing, and what systems they can access, then scaling quickly becomes a risk.” An AI Passport is a cryptographically signed credential for AI agents that is checked at runtime to verify the scope authorized by the enterprise. When an AI agent stays within its passport scope, it can operate freely, but if it tries to deviate, defined actions are enforced. These can include redirecting, restricting, or reconnecting the agent with proper context, or even triggering a kill switch. All actions are audited so agent activity can be tracked. It is built on open specifications, so any governance product, identity provider, or enforcement point can issue and verify credentials for their own and third-party AI agents, and those credentials are verifiable at every step in multi-agent workflows. A bouncer at every door This is a real step forward, said Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research. “Most agent governance today is a security camera. It records what happened so someone can review the tape later. AI Passport is a bouncer at every door.” The controls extend beyond ServiceNow’s own agents, he said: “For third-party agents, the passport replaces the agent’s own ‘claims’ about its permissions,” he said. “Taking an agent’s word for what it is allowed to do is an Achilles’ heel of agentic AI.” And, he said, “A passport

title: Google aims to make BigQuery spending on AI functions more predictable with token quotas
summary: Google has made daily token quotas generally available for BigQuery’s generative AI functions to give enterprises a way to limit AI consumption by project and individual user. These quotas, which can be managed via the IAM and Admin tab in the Google Cloud Console, cover both input and output tokens at the project and individual-user levels per day and apply to the AI.GENERATE, AI.GENERATE_TABLE, AI.GENERATE_TEXT, AI.CLASSIFY, AI.IF, AI.AGG, and AI.SCORE functions. Last year in November, the hyperscaler added AI-based SQL functions to its managed data warehouse and analytics platform to help enterprises reduce the complexity of running large-scale analytics, especially on unstructured data. These functions, which use LLMs to prepare unstructured data for analysis, reduce the traditionally time-consuming process of preparing such data because SQL cannot understand its nuances and meaning. However, embedding functions such as AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING , also available as ML.GENERATE_EMBEDDING and AI.EMBED are not subject to these quotas because they run on different, substantially cheaper models, the company wrote in a blog post . For the other functions, by default, input tokens are capped at 200 billion per project and 150 billion per user per day, while output tokens are capped at 20 billion per project and 15 billion per user per day. The output token quotas also include the reasoning tokens used by the LLM, the company wrote, adding that enterprises also have the option to raise a request to increase these default quotas. There is also the option to manage these quotas programmatically through the Cloud Quotas API , the gcloud CLI , and Terraform . How BigQuery enforces token quotas Beyond that, however, there are nuances to how the data warehouse platform enforces token quotas. title: Your AI agent needs more than memory. It needs reliable state
summary: Most teams building AI agents are pouring effort into better memory, longer context windows, conversation summaries, retrieval systems that pull up anything the agent has ever seen. These are useful tools. But they do not solve the problem of knowing whether an action actually completed. Memory tells an agent what happened. It doesn’t tell the agent what’s true right now. And for any agent that takes real action — refunding money, changing an order, updating an account — that distinction is the whole ballgame. Arjun Mullick Memory can remember a request without knowing the outcome Picture a customer service agent that approves a refund. The refund actually goes through, but the confirmation response times out before the agent hears back. From the agent’s point of view, all it has is a record of a request it made, not proof of what happened next. If the agent trusts its own memory, it sees an unfinished task and tries again. The reasoning is sound. The second refund is still wrong. More conversation history doesn’t fix this. What the agent needs is a record it can trust: the request ID, the current status, the confirmed outcome. Memory can tell you what the customer asked for. It can’t tell you what another system actually did. This isn’t a new problem; recommendation systems ran into a version of it years before agents existed. A prediction is not the same as current intent I spent several years building recommendation and personalization systems, and one thing became clear fast: more history doesn’t automatically mean a better decision. A recommender looks at what someone bought, browsed, or listened to, finds a pattern and predicts what they’ll want next. These are all informed guesses rather than facts. I saw this play out around election season. A customer buys several books about a candidate or a political topic and the system, correctly, learns that as an interest. title: Building Fabric Apps with Microsoft’s Rayfin
summary: Using vibe coding to scratch an itch has many of the same issues as using low-code and no-code development tools. That’s not surprising. Putting together something quickly to solve a specific problem lacks the level of discipline of software engineering, introducing inefficiencies that come from not following architectural guidelines and policies. I recently reviewed the AI-generated code I used to quickly build a PDF archive of some HTML-formatted content. The program used common libraries in unusual ways, often combining three or more libraries when all the necessary calls were in one, with a program flow that was hard to understand in places. The result was at best unmaintainable. The only way it was acceptable was that I’d thrown it together in an hour to solve a specific problem, and once I’d built that local PDF archive I could simply throw the program away. But what if your sloppy AI-generated code was needed by an entire department, or had become part of an essential business process? The risk is that something, somewhere, would inevitably change, and that essential business process would fail, with no practical way of fixing the code. The risk only compounds when the author has left their role and there is no one left who remembers or understands the initial prompts that produced the code. Adding AI-powered coding tools to products and platforms is risky. But they are too useful to ignore. Like low-code tools, AI tools put coding in the hands of the people who understand the business problems and helps them automate processes on their own schedule. What’s needed is a way to improve the harnesses used by the coding agents, taking concepts from specification-driven development and using them to build guardrails and standards into the code they produce, with the aim of building code that’s maintainable. title: When an agent acts, who is accountable?
summary: For most of the history of enterprise software, accountability has been relatively easy to understand. A person logs in, a person has a set of permissions, and a person takes an action. If something goes wrong, you can usually work backwards from there. Agentic AI changes that. We are moving from systems that suggest what someone should do to systems that can actually do it. Agents can access tools, call other systems, make decisions across multiple steps, and increasingly operate without a human approving every move. That is the point, of course. An autonomous system that needs someone hovering over every decision is not particularly autonomous. But the more action we hand over, the more important one deceptively simple question becomes: When an agent does something, who did it? Not philosophically. Operationally. Whose authority was it using? What was it allowed to touch? Who granted those permissions? And if something goes wrong, who owns the outcome? Accountability starts with identity The first question is what an agent actually is inside your organization. Should it always be treated as a delegate of a human, acting on that person’s behalf and inheriting some version of their permissions? That model makes accountability relatively straightforward. If my agent does something, the action can be traced back to me. But it becomes harder to sustain as agents become more persistent and autonomous. An agent might run continuously or serve an entire team rather than one person. It might perform a business function that continues long after whoever originally configured it has moved on. In those cases, should the agent have an identity of its own? And if it does, who creates that identity, who owns it, who grants its permissions, and how long should those permissions last? Identity is where accountability starts because if you cannot reliably answer who the agent is, everything that follows becomes harder to reason about. title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
summary: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from " people with knowledge of the matter ". Key things I learned from the article: Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn" Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power" Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11% This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine): The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones. When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending. Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter. Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter! Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" ( previously ) in these communications to their investors. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic

title: Chirp Pong
summary: Tool: Chirp Pong Another game experiment - I wanted to see if it was feasible to have a two player game on two separate phones running in static HTML where the networking code uses chirps sent via the microphone. It seems to work! Build a two player competitive pong like game where two players use their phones close to each other and the game state is sent via audio noises which the web microphone API can interpret - but add graphical and gameplay twists to make it a lot more fun and intertwine than pong Claude Opus 5.5 Extra in Claude Code . title: Four AI models, one ad, one clear winner.
summary: Four AI models, one ad, one clear winner. Here's which one gets the tiny label text right. Same FutureFuel can, same prompt, with every line of text spelled out along with where it should go. The can is covered in small print, which is exactly why it makes such a good test. -NanoBanana 2.1: "Even the 473 milliliter is super clear." Perfect text, nice light flares, good composition. -GPT Image 2.5: Text is crystal clear when you zoom in, but the design feels a little busy and generic. -Flux 3: A small error on the three. Really close, but it doesn't stand out like the other two. NanoBanana takes this one?

title: Gemini 4 Argon: AI Marketing, 3D Printing and SaaS
summary: Gemini 4 Argon is LIVE, Google's most advanced AI model, try it for yourself: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/gemini4-argon In this solo episode, I share what I learned after a week with Gemini 4 Argon, Google's new frontier model. I show three places it shines: marketing with AI, physical AI, and complex engineering, with a real build for each. You'll see Argon rebuild my holding company's website, write a post in my voice, design a Shopify product customizer that exports STL files, and build a free quoting app for commercial cleaning companies. I close with six techniques that raise Argon's output quality and the Google AI plan I'd pick for building.
